questions.q: Why does a web3 TypeScript project need `target` set to ES2020 or newer?
options: ES2020 is required for all import statements to work
bigint literals (like 2_500_000_000_000_000_000n) require target ES2020 or newer to compile
Older targets don't support the `strict` compiler flag
bigint as a type didn't exist before ES2020
questions.explain: bigint literals specifically require target ES2020+; the bigint type itself existed earlier (since TS 3.2), but the literal syntax (the trailing n) needs the newer target.

questions.q: Why does setting module/moduleResolution to "NodeNext" matter for a web3 project specifically?
options: NodeNext makes bigint literals compile on older targets
NodeNext disables strict mode automatically
Many web3 libraries ship ESM-only, and NodeNext resolves imports the way modern Node.js actually handles a package's "type" field and exports map
NodeNext is required to use JSON imports
questions.explain: Older CommonJS-style module resolution can silently break on ESM-only packages with a confusing "cannot find module" error; NodeNext resolves imports the way Node.js itself does.

questions.q: Which strict-mode flag forces code to handle nullable fields like `to: Address | null` on a Transaction interface?
options: skipLibCheck
resolveJsonModule
outDir
strictNullChecks
questions.explain: strictNullChecks is the flag that requires code to explicitly handle null/undefined cases instead of assuming a value is always present.

questions.q: What does skipLibCheck: true do, and why is it useful in a real project with many dependencies?
options: It skips checking your own source files for type errors
It skips type-checking inside .d.ts files from node_modules, so one outdated dependency's type definitions can't block the whole build
It disables bigint support
It automatically updates outdated npm packages
questions.explain: skipLibCheck only skips checking inside library .d.ts files (not your own code), preventing a single bad or outdated dependency type definition from blocking compilation.

questions.q: What does noUncheckedIndexedAccess change about reading `block.transactions[0]`?
options: It throws a runtime error if the array is empty
It automatically fills the array with a default value
It has no effect on array indexing, only on object properties
It types the result as `Hash | undefined` instead of assuming the array always has an element at that index
questions.explain: noUncheckedIndexedAccess (an opt-in flag, not bundled into strict) types any array index access as possibly undefined, which matters for something like a transactions array that could be empty.
